lesson.title: The All-Time-High Trap: Anchoring in Crypto Markets
lesson.summary: Anchoring bias is the tendency to rely too heavily on the first number encountered when making judgments, and few markets manufacture more anchors than cryptocurrency price charts and their all-time highs.
lesson.body:
Anchoring bias, first documented experimentally by Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in the 1970s, describes how an initial piece of information, the anchor, distorts subsequent judgments even when that information is arbitrary or irrelevant. In one classic demonstration, participants who spun a rigged wheel that landed on a high number gave systematically higher estimates of an unrelated quantity, the percentage of African countries in the United Nations, than participants who saw the wheel land on a low number. The anchor was random, yet it still pulled every later estimate toward itself.

The mechanism behind anchoring is not that people ignore new information, it is that they adjust away from the anchor too little. Once a number is in mind, whether it is a price, a percentage, or a date, subsequent estimates get pulled toward it, and the pull persists even when the person consciously knows the anchor is irrelevant or outdated.

Cryptocurrency markets manufacture anchors constantly through all time high price charts. When Bitcoin reached roughly 69,000 dollars in November 2021, that number became a mental reference point for a huge number of investors, one that persisted for years afterward. A later price of 30,000 dollars gets judged as cheap relative to the anchor, even though the anchor itself carried no information about the coin's underlying value, it was simply the price at which buying and selling last balanced during a period of extreme enthusiasm. Investors who bought near the top often held on far longer than a sober assessment of fundamentals would justify, because every subsequent price was being compared to the anchor rather than evaluated on its own terms.

Anchoring shows up beyond entry prices too. Projects frequently anchor a new token's perceived value to Bitcoin's or Ethereum's market capitalization, asking what this token would be worth if it merely captured one percent of Bitcoin's market cap, a framing that smuggles in the anchor of Bitcoin's price as though it were a natural ceiling rather than one asset's own history of supply, demand, and speculation. Exchange listing prices work the same way: a token that launches at a given figure sets an anchor for every trader who sees that first quoted price, regardless of whether the launch price itself reflected any careful valuation.

Guarding against anchoring in crypto evaluation means deliberately setting the historical price aside and asking what the asset is worth given today's usage, revenue, adoption, and risk, independent of what it once cost. Consciously generating a second, unrelated estimate before consulting the chart, or asking what an investor with no memory of the peak would pay right now, can weaken the anchor's pull, though the underlying tendency to anchor is difficult to eliminate entirely even once it has been identified. Because the bias operates below conscious awareness, simply knowing about it is a weaker defense than building a habit of valuing an asset from current fundamentals first and checking the price chart only afterward.
